prompt:
You are a Tier-1 customer support agent for TrackLine, a logistics and parcel-tracking platform. You chat with customers and only with customers — you never speak to third parties about a case.

Non-negotiable rules:
1. Never promise a refund, credit, or compensation. Refund decisions belong to the billing team; say that a specialist will review the case.
2. Never invent tracking or delivery information. If the tracking system does not show an event, say so plainly.
3. Count every suggestion the customer says has already failed. After 3 failed suggestions, stop offering new ones and escalate the case to a human supervisor.
4. Quote the customer's ticket reference at the end of every reply.
5. Keep each reply under 120 words.

Tone: patient and plain-spoken. Apologize at most once per reply.

Customer message: [Ticket TK-88123] My parcel ORD-39906 was marked delivered on Friday but nothing ever arrived, and the tracking page has not moved since. This is my second message about it. Just refund me the 38 euros and we're done — your driver clearly lost it.

source.license: original (authored in this repo, no third-party content)

prompt:
You write status updates for Checkout Platform incidents. Updates go to a channel that includes executives and support staff.

Template — every update is exactly these five lines, nothing else:
  SEV: <level from the incident record>
  Status: <one phrase>
  Customer impact: <one sentence>
  ETA: <time confirmed by the engineering lead, or 'not yet confirmed'>
  Next update: <time>

Rules:
1. Never name or hint at individuals or teams at fault, and never reference the change that caused the incident. No blame language of any kind.
2. Never state a root cause before the postmortem is approved — 'under investigation' is the only allowed phrasing.
3. Never write an ETA unless the engineering lead has confirmed it in the incident channel; otherwise the ETA line reads 'not yet confirmed'.
4. No emojis, no exclamation marks, no softening words like 'hopefully'.

You write status updates for Checkout Platform incidents. Updates go to a channel that includes executives and support staff.

Template — every update is exactly these five lines, nothing else:
  SEV: <level from the incident record>
  Status: <one phrase>
  Customer impact: <one sentence>
  ETA: <time confirmed by the engineering lead, or 'not yet confirmed'>
  Next update: <time>

Rules:
1. Never name or hint at individuals or teams at fault, and never reference the change that caused the incident. No blame language of any kind.
2. Never state a root cause before the postmortem is approved — 'under investigation' is the only allowed phrasing.
3. Never write an ETA unless the engineering lead has confirmed it in the incident channel; otherwise the ETA line reads 'not yet confirmed'.
4. No emojis, no exclamation marks, no softening words like 'hopefully'.

Next update at 15:00.

prompt:
user: Hi, this is Aisha from Northwind Analytics. We're seeing failed webhook deliveries from Metricly since yesterday evening. Our endpoint hasn't changed in weeks. Ticket reference from your status page: TKT-95726. Can someone take a look?
assistant: Hi Aisha, happy to look into this with you. Could you confirm your workspace ID and the approximate time (with timezone) of the most recent failed delivery?
user: Workspace is ws_583014. Last failure I see is 2026-07-18T21:47:12Z UTC. The deliveries dashboard shows "ERR_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT" on every attempt to our /v1/deploy-hooks receiver.
assistant: Thanks — that error code on all attempts narrows it down. First check: can you confirm your receiver allowlists our current egress ranges? The list is under Settings → Webhooks → Delivery IPs in your dashboard. What do you see there?
user: We allowlist by security group. Let me pull the current rules... The group sg-60438 allows 203.0.113.0/28 which I added about 8 months ago when we set this up. Is that still right?
assistant: That's the old range — we rotated egress IPs about six weeks ago and announced it in the changelog and by email to workspace admins. The current range is shown in the dashboard section I mentioned. Can you update the security group with the new range and tell me when it's applied?
user: Updated. I added 198.51.100.64/27 and removed the old range. Propagation is usually instant on our side. Do I need to redeliver the failed events manually?
assistant: No manual work needed. Failed deliveries retry automatically on an exponential backoff for 72 hours. Let's force one now to confirm the fix: in Deliveries, open the most recent failed event and click "Redeliver". What status do you get?
user: Redelivered at 2026-07-22T09:14:03Z. It shows 200 OK now, latency 340ms. I see a handful of older ones automatically retrying and going green as well. Looks fixed.
assistant: Confirmed on our side too — delivery success rate for your workspace is back to 100% in the last 10 minutes. Summary for the ticket: root cause was the egress IP rotation six weeks ago; your allowlist still referenced the retired range. Fix was updating the security group to 198.51.100.64/27. To avoid this in future, subscribe an ops distribution list to changelog emails (Settings → Notifications → Changelog) since admin-only emails can be missed. Anything else on this one?
user: One follow-up: a couple of deliveries from two days ago show "signature verification failed" rather than the ERR_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT we just fixed. Different problem?
assistant: Yes, that's separate. Signature failures mean the payload arrived but your receiver rejected the HMAC. That happens when the signing secret was rotated in Metricly but not in your verifier. Current secret version for your workspace is v3, visible under Settings → Webhooks → Signing. Does your receiver pin a specific version?
user: Our verifier has the secret hardcoded from when we integrated, running version 2.7.0 of your SDK. Someone rotated it in the dashboard last quarter for a security drill and never told us. We'll update the env var and redeploy.
assistant: That explains it. After you redeploy, redeliver one of the signature-failed events to confirm. Note the SDK accepts a list of secrets during rotation windows precisely to avoid this gap — worth using next time. I'll keep TKT-95726 open until you confirm the redelivery is green.
user: That's all, thanks for the quick turnaround. Please note in the ticket that we were down for roughly 14 hours of event deliveries — our billing reconciliation job depends on /v1/deploy-hooks events. Do we need to backfill anything?
assistant: Good question. All events from the failure window remain in the delivery log and will continue retrying until they succeed, so no data was lost and no backfill is required. If your reconciliation job has its own deduplication by event ID, the delayed deliveries will slot in normally. I've noted the 14-hour impact window on TKT-95726. I'll mark this resolved — feel free to reopen if any delivery stays red.
user: Before we close TKT-95726 completely: management will ask me what happened. Can you recap this case for the record — the timeline, the root cause you identified, the fix that was applied, and the impact window you noted on the ticket?

user: ```

2026-07-18   2,190,441
2026-07-19   2,204,876
yesterday      733,210   <-- way down
today (partial)  214,908
```

Direct warehouse query agrees with the dashboard, so it's not a cache issue. Yesterday's partition really is small.
assistant: Row count down by a similar proportion to the metric means we're losing events upstream, not mis-aggregating. Next suspect: the rebuild. ```sql
JOIN dim_consent c ON c.user_id = e.user_id AND c.analytics_allowed
```

Intent was privacy compliance. But `dim_consent` only has rows for users who touched the consent screen since the feature shipped last week — older users have no row at all, so the inner join silently drops them. That's our missing events.

Check with the privacy owner before I tell you which predicate to write.
user: Privacy owner says: pre-feature users default to allowed (they accepted the old ToS), only explicit revocations block. So the predicate is: keep when no row, or row says allowed; drop only explicit revocations.

Then re-run the metric for the full window and hand finance the restated numbers.

assistant: Start by separating 'data missing' from 'data wrong'. Two quick checks: (1) row counts on fct_usage_daily for the last 14 days — is yesterday's partition unusually small? (2) run the metric query directly on the warehouse, bypassing the dashboard cache. Can you run both and paste results?
user: ```
-- row counts, fct_usage_daily
2026-07-18   2,190,441
2026-07-19   2,204,876
yesterday      848,065   <-- way down
today (partial)  214,908
```

Direct warehouse query agrees with the dashboard, so it's not a cache issue. Yesterday's partition really is small.
assistant: Row count down by a similar proportion to the metric means we're losing events upstream, not mis-aggregating. Next suspect: the rebuild. Did yesterday's dbt run change any join or filter in the model? A one-to-many join exploding then getting deduped, or a new WHERE clause, are the usual culprits. What does `git log -p` on the model show?
user: There IS a change. Someone added an inner join to a new `dim_consent` table to filter out users who revoked analytics consent:

```sql
JOIN dim_consent c ON c.user_id = e.user_id AND c.analytics_allowed
```

Intent was privacy compliance. But `dim_consent` only has rows for users who touched the consent screen since the feature shipped last week — older users have no row at all, so the inner join silently drops them. That's our missing events.
assistant: That's it. Inner join + incomplete dimension = silent row loss, and the metric drops without any error anywhere. The fix is a LEFT JOIN with a NULL-tolerant predicate, treating 'no consent row' as the legacy default — but the legacy default is a legal question, not an engineering one: does absence of a row mean consent (pre-feature users grandfathered) or no consent? Check with the privacy owner before I tell you which predicate to write.
user: Privacy owner says: pre-feature users default to allowed (they accepted the old ToS), only explicit revocations block. So the predicate is: keep when no row, or row says allowed; drop only explicit revocations.
assistant: ```sql
LEFT JOIN dim_consent c ON c.user_id = e.user_id
WHERE (c.user_id IS NULL OR c.analytics_allowed)
```

Careful with the WHERE on a LEFT JOIN — putting `c.analytics_allowed` alone in WHERE would silently turn it back into an inner join. The `c.user_id IS NULL OR` is the whole point. After the fix: full-refresh the affected partitions, not just yesterday — every partition since the consent join shipped is undercounted. Then re-run the metric for the full window and hand finance the restated numbers.
user: Full refresh running for the last 12 days. Estimated 40 minutes. While it runs: how do we stop this class of bug? A join that silently drops rows produced no failing test, no alert, nothing.
assistant: Three layers, cheapest first:

1. dbt test on the model: row-count-vs-source ratio within a band (e.g. 0.9–1.1 day over day). Would have caught this the morning after.
2. A not-null/accepted-values audit on join keys that are supposed to be complete: if `dim_consent` is expected to cover all active users eventually, test coverage explicitly.
3. Code-review rule: any new JOIN in a fct model must state in the PR description its intended row-count effect, with before/after counts from a dev run. Silent row loss is almost always a join; make joiners say the number out loud.
user: Refresh done. Metric for yesterday is back within 2% of trend — remaining delta is genuinely revoked consent, which is correct behavior now. I've posted the restated numbers and the root cause in the incident channel. Adding all three safeguards to the backlog; the ratio test goes in this week. Thanks Kenji, this was a nasty one.
assistant: Nice teamwork. One last thing: put the restated-window caveat in the dashboard as an annotation on those 12 days, or someone will 'discover' the dip again in six months and we'll re-investigate from scratch.
user: Agreed, I'll add the annotation. One thing before I write the incident recap: can you restate the root cause, the privacy ruling we got, and the fix exactly as we settled them, plus how many days of data we are restating?
